title: Fine-tuning
note: The fine-tuning argument starts from physics, not biology: several constants and initial conditions seem to fall in narrow ranges that permit life. The usual options are physical necessity, chance, or design. Critics appeal to observation selection effects and to a multiverse; defenders reply that neither removes the need for explanation.

read.title: Necessity, chance, or design
text: Physicists have noted that several features of the universe seem balanced on a knife-edge. The vacuum energy, or cosmological constant, is vastly smaller than theory would suggest, yet much larger values would prevent galaxies from forming. Changes to the strong nuclear force would upset the formation of the elements. Roger Penrose estimated the improbability of the universe's low initial entropy at one part in ten to the power ten to the 123.
The argument can be set out:
(1) The fine-tuning of the universe for life is due to physical necessity, chance, or design. (2) It is not due to physical necessity. (3) It is not due to chance. (4) Therefore it is due to design.

The leading objection targets premise (3). If there are vast numbers of universes with different constants, as some versions of inflation and string theory suggest, then a few will permit life, and observers will naturally find themselves in one of those. Fine-tuning would then be no more surprising than a lottery having a winner.

Defenders reply in several ways. Roger White argues that other universes do not raise the probability that this universe permits life. Robin Collins argues that any known mechanism for generating universes would itself need finely set laws. Others note that the multiverse remains a speculative hypothesis with problems of its own, such as Boltzmann brains. Critics answer that a multiverse may still be the better bet, since it is suggested by physics itself.
